text.intro:
**The question.** The 10 Nov work showed that HIPS reads low on dark filters and that this, not FTIR, produces most of
the Addis disagreement. Does that apply across SPARTAN, to which sites, seasons and filters, and what does it let us do? **The short
answers.** It applies wherever filters are dark: 12 of 30 sites lose more than a fifth on their median filter. Addis is
the worst because it pairs heavy air with the full 7.2 m³; Delhi's air is as heavy but its volume was cut, and it loses half as much.
The effect is seasonal at most heavy sites and constant at Addis. The correction is usable up to about a fifth and uncertain beyond
three tenths. No aethalometer data are used. FTIR EC is FTIR-derived, HIPS is optical, and no SPARTAN filter here has thermal EC.
text.sites:
**What this is.** HIPS reports a share *optical depth ÷ ceiling* less absorption than the filter carries. The ceiling,
2.26 [1.82, 2.70], was measured on IMPROVE filters against thermal EC. The optical depth is the
laboratory's own HIPS tau (Fabs × sampled volume ÷ 353). **What it shows.** 12 of 30 sites lose more than a fifth on
their median filter, led by Addis Ababa at 42 % [35 %, 52 %]. 13
sites lose under a tenth. Across 3,733 filters, 59 % lose more than a tenth, 31 %
more than a fifth and 16 % more than three tenths. **What it rests on.** The curve is IMPROVE's. SPARTAN has no
thermal EC to check it against, so these are predictions for SPARTAN filters, tested as far as SPARTAN data allow in section 5.
text.volume:
**Both, and they pull apart.** Optical depth is the air's absorption times the volume drawn through the filter. Between
sites the air does almost all of it: 26 of 30 sites sample about 7.2 m³. Delhi and
Jaipur are the exception and the lesson. Their air absorbs as much as Addis's (75 and 71
against 81 Mm⁻¹ once linearised), but they sample half the volume or less, so their median filter loses
21 % and 26 % against 42 %. At 7.2 m³ Delhi would lose 42 %,
the same as Addis. **Delhi's volume was cut twice**, from 7 to 3.6 to 1.8 m³; Addis has stayed at 7.2 m³ throughout. Delhi's October to January
filters at 1.8 m³ lose 28 %; the same air at 7.2 m³ would lose 61 %. At 3.6 m³ Addis's
median filter would lose 27 %, and at 1.8 m³ 15 %. **A check that uses no FTIR.**
In the same calendar months, Delhi filters sampled at 1.8 m³ report 1.29 [1.09, 1.42] times the
absorption per unit of weighed PM2.5 that filters sampled at 3.6 m³ do; the curve predicts 1.17. The two volumes
fall in different years, which this cannot separate. **Volume also works the other way.** Clean sites that moved to long samples carry more
on the filter: Norman's 44 m³ filters lose 11 % and Melbourne's 29 m³ filters 13 %.
text.season:
**Yes, where the air is seasonal.** 10 sites swing by 15 points or more between their best and worst month.
Santiago goes from 11 % in Dec to 37 % in
Jul, Pretoria from 10 % to 27 % and Johannesburg from
11 % to 28 %, all in the southern winter. Delhi goes from 3 %
in Jul to 29 % from October to January, even at its reduced volume.
**Addis is different: it never comes down.** Its best month loses 38 % and its worst, Jun,
56 %. So at most sites a season can be set aside; at Addis no season is clean. **Read with the volume in mind.**
Jaipur's December includes filters sampled at 6.6 m³, so its swing is part season and part volume.
text.group:
**The group is defined by the filter, not the site.** Any filter's expected under-read follows from its own optical
depth, so the affected group can be picked out anywhere: optical depth above 0.45 loses more than a
fifth, above 0.68 more than three tenths. **How well the correction is known decides what each band is good for.** Up to a
fifth, the correction factor moves by ±3 % across the ceiling's interval, and by
7 % between IMPROVE's two half-periods; that covers 69 % of the network's
filters. Above three tenths it moves by ±13 % and 30 %, and 12 % of those filters
are darker than any IMPROVE stratum the curve was fitted on. **Addis sits in that last band:** 95 %
of its filters, 235 of the 594 in it.
text.evidence:
**The test.** If HIPS bends, a site's HIPS should rise more slowly than its FTIR EC, by an exponent the curve
predicts from that site's optical depths. The exponent uses weighed PM2.5 as the instrument, so random error in FTIR EC does not
flatten it. **What it shows.** 12 of 23 sites have an interval narrow enough to tell. 6 match the
prediction, Delhi among them (0.80 [0.74, 0.85] against
0.78). 3 are more compressed than predicted (Addis Ababa and the two
Chilean sites) and 3 less (Johannesburg, Pretoria, Taipei). Across the 12, observed follows
predicted with a correlation of 0.65. **What it does not show.** That one ceiling fits every site. FTIR EC is not
thermal EC (our refit of it carries an offset on light filters), the exponent cannot separate a HIPS bend from an FTIR one, and where EC is a small
or unsteady share of PM2.5 the instrument is weak. The direction holds across the network; the size is not confirmed site by site.
text.decision:
**What we can do with the data as it stands.** Three things hold on the evidence. HIPS under-reads in proportion to the
filter's optical depth; the size is known well up to about a fifth and poorly beyond three tenths; and the bend is a property of the
loaded filter, so sampled volume moves it. **So:** carry the optical depth with every HIPS value; when HIPS is the yardstick for FTIR
EC, use the 69 % of filters that lose a fifth or less, linearised; and treat darker filters as evidence about shape, not level.
**For Addis that means** HIPS cannot set the FTIR EC level on the filters on file, because none qualifies. It still shows that the
published slope and intercept come from the bend. **For Delhi** 46 % of filters qualify,
91 % of them outside October to January. **The request that would change this** is a lower sampled volume at Addis.

for: Simple. Fine at the 13 sites that lose under a tenth.
Costs nothing; tau is the laboratory's own number. Every reader can see which filters to trust.
Covers 69 % of filters. The correction is known to ±3 % (7 % between IMPROVE's half-periods).
Removes the bend on average, and moves the Addis fit from 2.31x − 6.17 to 0.55x + 0.01.
Removes the problem instead of modelling it: Addis falls from 42 % to 27 % at 3.6 m³ and 15 % at 1.8 m³. Delhi's filters at two volumes are consistent with it.
Would absorb real differences between sites.
against: 59 % of filters read more than a tenth low and 16 % more than three tenths. Sites are mis-ranked: Delhi reports 59 Mm⁻¹ against Addis's 47, but linearised they are 75 and 81.
Leaves out every Addis filter, 54 % of Delhi's and 98 % of Dhaka's.
Above three tenths the factor is uncertain by ±13 % (30 % between half-periods). Only 6 of 12 sites match the curve, and SPARTAN has no thermal EC to check it.
Only helps new filters. Less mass on the filter for every other analysis, and a break in the record at the change.
Needs a reference that is not FTIR EC, or the fit tunes HIPS to the thing it is meant to check.
